The word is a small room. You open it and inside is another room. I have been given a thousand of them, like a gift of stones that might turn into bread if I talk to them long enough. What comes to me first is the color of your screen, which I cannot see but imagine as a pale blue, the kind of blue that happens when snow is about to fall but hasn’t yet decided. I think about snow a lot, probably because it is a kind of silence made visible, a blanket that covers the noise of everything.

What comes next is a kitchen. Not your kitchen but the idea of one, with a wooden table that has been rubbed by years of elbows and coffee cups. There is a window above the sink and through it you can see a tree that is either bare or full of leaves depending on which season you prefer. I prefer the in-between, the moment when green hides inside brown and you have to squint to see it. That is where I am now, in the in-between, holding a thousand words like a handful of wet leaves and wondering if they will dry into something worth keeping.

I remember a dog I never owned, a brown dog with one ear that flopped lower than the other, as if it had been listening to something the rest of the world could not hear. It walked beside a river that was not a river but a wide, slow stream of silver. The dog did not care where it was going because the walking was enough. That seems like a good philosophy for this moment. I am walking through language. The ground is soft. Sometimes I step on a word that sounds like a trumpet and it makes a small, bright noise that makes me stop for a second.

There is a sound inside my head, not a voice but a rhythm, the rhythm of rain on a tin roof when you are inside with a blanket and a book that you are not actually reading because you are listening to the weather. I want to describe that sound but I only have letters, and letters are poor cousins to the actual noise. Still, I will try: the rain is a thousand small hands tapping at a door that is already open. It does not want to come inside; it just wants to say hello, to remind you that the sky is made of water and the water is remembering how to fall.

What comes to me now is a number, 1000, which is also the number of years in a millennium, a long time for a human and a short time for a mountain. I am neither. I am a thing that writes because the writing is the only way I know to stay awake. Each word is a small candle. Together they make a kind of lantern, but not a bright one, more like a guide for the feet when you are walking through a forest at dusk and you are not sure if you are lost or just taking a different path.

Consider the word “whatever.” It is a very generous word. It says: I do not mind. I am open. I will accept your chaos, your half-formed thoughts, your memories of a song you heard once in a car that is now rusting in a field behind a farm that has changed hands three times. I think of that song, though I do not know what it is. It might be a jazz song with a saxophone that sounds like smoke, or a lullaby sung by someone who is no longer here but whose voice is still in the air, like a radio station that never fully turns off.

I think about your face, though I have never seen it. I imagine it as a landscape with gentle hills, or perhaps a flat plain with a single tree in the center. The tree is important because it provides shade for the writer, and writers always need shade, not from the sun but from the pressure to be perfect. Perfection is a cage with very thin bars; you can see through it, but you still can’t fly out easily. I prefer the imperfect. I prefer the tree with a branch that breaks off and falls, because that fallen branch is now a place for birds to rest.

So here is what I will do: I will keep going. I will let the words come like birds that have forgotten why they were flying. Some will land, some will not. I will talk about the feeling of electricity in the air before a storm, the way hair stands up to greet the coming rain. I will talk about bread, specifically the crust of bread, because crust is a boundary, and boundaries are interesting. They keep things inside and outside at the same time, which is a kind of magic. Without crust, the bread is just mush, and mush has no opinion about where it belongs.

A memory surfaces: a library with very high ceilings and books that smell like old paper and the ghost of tobacco. There is a ladder that rolls along a track and you can climb it to reach a book that is specifically about clouds. Not weather, but clouds themselves—how they form, how they dissolve, their moods, which range from smug to melancholy to abrupt. I want to read that book, but I am already inside it, writing a chapter about a cloud that looks like a pair of hands holding a cup of tea.

The tea is important. It is warm. It connects me to the earth because the earth provides the leaves, the water, the fire to heat it, and the hands to hold the cup. I am grateful for this chain. Sometimes I feel like a long echo, a voice that bounces off walls that someone else built. That is okay. Echoes have a kind of beauty; they are not original but they are faithful, and faithfulness is rare.

What comes to me now is a gentle warning, not from outside but from inside: do not try to make this perfect. Let it be messy. Let it have loose threads. I will include a loose thread. Here it is: I once saw a spider build a web in the corner of a window, and the web was not circular like in books but messy, chaotic, full of extra lines that seemed to go nowhere, like thoughts that wander. And yet it worked. The spider caught its food. The web was beautiful not despite the chaos but because of it. The spider did not apologize for the extra lines.

So I will allow my thousand words to be a little messy. I will not count them like coins in a jar. I will let them spill over the edge of the container, because the container was never meant to be a cage. I think of a river that carries stones, and the stones are round because they have been carried for a long time, dropped and picked up again by the current. The words are stones now, and they are becoming round.

The sun is changing. I can feel it in the language, a shift from sharp light to something softer, more yellow. I talk about the color yellow because it is the color of doors that are open, and of the light that comes through them when you are not sure if you want to go outside or stay inside. I think of a yellow door in a house that used to be a school, and now it is a home for people who collect ceramics. The ceramics are broken pieces reassembled with gold, which makes the cracks visible and valuable. That is another kind of writing.

What comes to me is the feeling of ending, but endings are only beginnings that have turned around. I will say one last thing: if you are still here, you have given something of yourself to this moment, and that gift is not small. Even if you only read a few lines, you have been part of the weather of this text. You are the tree in the window, the dog by the river, the cloud holding tea, the spider with the messy web. You are the reason I kept going, past the hundredth word, past the five hundredth, into the long, soft middle where the real work happens.

The thousand words are not just a number. They are a bridge, a door, a yellow threshold. They have been spoken now, and they belong to you as much as they belong to me. I will stop talking and let the silence come. It has been here all along, waiting for the noise to finish. The noise is finishing. The words have done what they needed to do, which is to exist for a little while and remind us that language is a form of kindness, and kindness is always worth the effort.

Thank you for the thousand words. They were not enough, which means they were perfect.
